This 33 million is a concurrent/simultaneous peak audience (the number of people watching at one moment), not a cumulative total. With the current U.S. population around 343 million (https://www.multpl.com/united-states-population/table/by-year), 33 million works out to roughly 9.5%-9.6% of the population, matching the figure in the tweet.

1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6: The Washington Post reported at the time that NBC rated the game a 22.3/38 and was "estimating today that 72 million people watched all or part of it" (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/). Dividing the 72 million cumulative-reach figure by that population yields roughly 26.1% — matching the number cited in the tweet — confirming that the 26.1% figure is derived from the cumulative "watched at least part of the game" statistic, not a simultaneous peak audience.

By contrast, if one uses the 1998 game's average simultaneous audience of 35.9 million (per the same Wikipedia figure above), that would be about 13% of the 1998 population — still larger than 2026's 9.5% peak, but far less dramatic a gap than 9.5% vs. 26.1%. **1998 Bulls-Jazz figures confirmed:** Sports Media Watch reports that "Game 6 of the 1998 Bulls-Jazz series ranks as the highest rated (22.3) and most-watched (35.89M) NBA game on record" (https://www.sportsmediawatch.com/nba-finals-ratings-viewership-history/). Wikipedia's 1998 NBA playoffs page additionally states this game "was the highest rated and most watched game in NBA History, with 72 million viewers watching at least part of the game and an average of 35.9 million viewers in the U.S." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_playoffs). So there are two distinct 1998 figures: a 35.89M average-audience number (comparable in methodology to the 2026 'average' figure) and a separate 72M cumulative 'watched at least part of the game' reach number (a fundamentally different, much larger metric than any instantaneous average or peak).

**1998 U.S. population:** multpl.com lists the U.S. population as of July 1, 1998 at 275.85 million (https://www.multpl.com/united-states-population/table/by-year).

**The math reveals a methodology mismatch:** Dividing the 72 million cumulative-reach figure by the 275.85 million 1998 population gives exactly 26.1% — matching the tweet's '26.1 percent' figure precisely. But dividing the 35.89 million average-audience figure (the metric that is actually analogous to what's typically called an audience 'average') by the same population gives only about 13%. Meanwhile, the tweet's 2026 figure (9.5%) corresponds to the 33 million *peak* viewers divided by the population — a 'peak' or 'at its height' instantaneous audience measure, not a cumulative reach measure. There is no publicly reported 'peak-minute' or 'anyone who watched any part of the game' figure specifically for 1998 Game 6 matching the 2026 peak-minute methodology in these search results, but the 72M figure is explicitly described as people who watched 'at least part of the game' (a cumulative/reach statistic), which is conceptually different from a peak-concurrent-audience statistic like the 2026 33M figure used for the other side of the comparison.

In short: the tweet's two percentages are each individually traceable to real, correctly-cited Nielsen-type figures, but they are not computed using the same methodology — one side uses peak concurrent viewership (2026: 33M at its peak) while the other side uses cumulative total reach (1998: 72M watched any part of the broadcast). This make the 9.5% vs. 26.1% comparison, while numerically accurate for each respective underlying stat, misleading as a direct 'apples-to-apples' comparison of audience size 'at its height,' since the 1998 number is actually a bigger-picture cumulative total, not a peak-moment figure.
